{{short description|Statistical method to visualise the onset of an outbreak}}
{{broader| Mathematical modelling of infectious disease }}
An '''epidemic curve''', also known as an '''epi curve''' or '''epidemiological curve''', is a statistical [[chart]] used in [[epidemiology]] to visualise the onset of a [[Outbreak|disease outbreak]]. It can help with the identification of the mode of [[Transmission (medicine)|transmission]] of the disease. It can also show the disease's magnitude, whether cases are clustered or if there are individual case outliers, its trend over time, and its incubation period.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://sphweb.bumc.bu.edu/otlt/MPH-Modules/EP/EP713_DescriptiveEpi/EP713_DescriptiveEpi3.html|title=Epidemic Curves|website=sphweb.bumc.bu.edu|access-date=2020-02-20}}</ref><ref name=":0" /> It can give outbreak investigators an idea as to whether an outbreak is likely to be from a [[point source (outbreak investigation)|point source]] (such as from a food handler), a [[continuous common source|continuous common]] source (with ongoing contamination), or a [[propagated source]] (that is transmitted primarily between people).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cdc.gov/training/QuickLearns/epimode/|title=Using an Epi Curve to Determine Mode of Spread|website=Centers for Disease Control and Prevention}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://sphweb.bumc.bu.edu/otlt/MPH-Modules/EP/EP713_DescriptiveEpi/EP713_DescriptiveEpi3.html|title=Epidemic Curves|last=LaMorte|first=Wayne W.|date=2017-05-05|website=Descriptive Epidemiology|publisher=Boston University School of Public Health|access-date=2020-02-20}}</ref>

Epidemic curves generally show the frequency of new cases compared to the date of disease onset.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://nciph.sph.unc.edu/focus/vol1/issue5/1-5EpiCurves_issue.pdf|title=Focus on Field Epidemiology|last=Torok|first=Michelle|date=2003|publisher=North Carolina Center for Public Health Preparedness}}</ref>

== Examples ==

=== Hepatitis A ===
[[File:Epidemic curve of Hepatitis A Nov-Dec 1978.jpg|frame|Common source outbreak of Hepatitis A in Nov-Dec 1978]]
This epidemic curve shows a presumed first case, known as the index case on November 6, 1978. 4 days later, there was a steep increase in cases, followed by the curve tapering down to zero. Some cases were food handlers, and some secondary cases. It showed that this is probably a common source outbreak. Sometimes, cases could have been exposed days or weeks prior, and diseases with longer incubation periods would flatten these epidemic curves and lower the peaks.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2020-05-11|title=Principles of Epidemiology {{!}} Lesson 1 - Section 11|url=https://www.cdc.gov/csels/dsepd/ss1978/lesson1/section11.html|access-date=2020-09-17|website=www.cdc.gov|language=en-us}}</ref>

=== COVID-19 pandemic ===
{{See also|Flatten the curve|Social distancing}}
The first description of epidemiological curves from the [[COVID-19 pandemic]] showed the pattern of a "mixed outbreak". According to the investigators, there was likely a continuous common source outbreak at Wuhan Seafood Market in December 2019, potentially from several [[zoonotic]] events. As of the date of publication of the study, it is unknown which animal may have been the original reservoir of the virus, or how it was originally transmitted to humans. Following this, the investigators found that the outbreak likely became a propagated source, meaning that the virus became able to be transmitted from person to person.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Zhang|first=Yanping|date=2020-02-14|title=The Novel Coronavirus Pneumonia Emergency Response Epidemiology Team. The Epidemiological Characteristics of an Outbreak of 2019 Novel Coronavirus Diseases (COVID-19) - China, 2020|url=http://weekly.chinacdc.cn/fileCCDCW/journal/article/ccdcw/newcreate/COVID-19.pdf|journal=China CDC Weekly|volume=2|access-date=2020-02-20|archive-date=2020-02-20|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200220200921/http://weekly.chinacdc.cn/fileCCDCW/journal/article/ccdcw/newcreate/COVID-19.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref> ''[[The New York Times]]'' has published a curve simulator for both the US and the world, on which the visitor can tinker the base parameters to get various outcomes.<ref>{{Cite news|last1=Kristof|first1=Nicholas|url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2020/03/25/opinion/coronavirus-trump-reopen-america.html|title=Opinion {{!}} Trump Wants to 'Reopen America.' Here's What Happens if We Do.|date=2020-03-25|work=The New York Times|access-date=2020-04-10|last2=Thompson|first2=Stuart A.|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref>
